items.readable_text:
Content:
Solving a linear equation involves isolating the variable on one side of the equation.

Content:
This can often be accomplished using the addition principle. The addition principle tells us that adding (or subtracting) the same number on both sides of an equation does not change its solution.

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to solve the equation
[MATH: x + 4 = 5.]

Content:
The variable [MATH: x] is not isolated, because we also have a [MATH: +4] on the left-hand side.

Content:
To isolate [MATH: x], we can perform the opposite operation, which is subtracting [MATH: 4] from [MATH: x.] This way, the [MATH: +4] and [MATH: -4] will cancel out to [MATH: 0,] which will leave [MATH: x] alone. Remember to do this to both sides of the equation!

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x + 4 &= 5 \
x+4\,{\color{red}{-}}\,{\color{red}{4}} &=5\,{\color{red}{-}}\,{\color{red}{4}} \
x+(4-4) &=(5-4) \
x + 0 &= 1 \
x &= 1.
}]

Content:
So [MATH: x=1] is our solution. Let's check that our solution is correct by plugging it back into the original equation:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x + 4 &= 5 \
1 + 4&= 5 \
5 &=5 \;{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Solving a linear equation involves isolating the variable on one side of the equation.

Content:
This can often be accomplished using the addition principle. The addition principle tells us that adding (or subtracting) the same number on both sides of an equation does not change its solution.

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to solve the equation
[MATH: x + 4 = 5.]

Content:
The variable [MATH: x] is not isolated, because we also have a [MATH: +4] on the left-hand side.

Content:
To isolate [MATH: x], we can perform the opposite operation, which is subtracting [MATH: 4] from [MATH: x.] This way, the [MATH: +4] and [MATH: -4] will cancel out to [MATH: 0,] which will leave [MATH: x] alone. Remember to do this to both sides of the equation!

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x + 4 &= 5 \
x+4\,{\color{red}{-}}\,{\color{red}{4}} &=5\,{\color{red}{-}}\,{\color{red}{4}} \
x+(4-4) &=(5-4) \
x + 0 &= 1 \
x &= 1.
}]

Content:
So [MATH: x=1] is our solution. Let's check that our solution is correct by plugging it back into the original equation:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x + 4 &= 5 \
1 + 4&= 5 \
5 &=5 \;{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
}]
